summary: This is a Docker cleanup wizard script written in Zsh that removes unused Docker resources (containers, images, volumes, and build cache). It scans your Docker environment, displays what will be deleted in a formatted execution plan, and either prompts you for confirmation on each step or auto-confirms everything if the force flag is set. The script supports two cleanup modes: standard (dangling images only) and deep clean (all unused images), selected via command-line flags.

explanations.4: This calls a helper function _d_check_env to verify that Docker is installed and available; if it's not found, the entire script exits early with return code 1.
explanations.10: This defines a local function that will only exist within this script's scope, not globally—it's used to print formatted help text when the user runs the script with --help or invalid options.
explanations.26: This begins a loop that processes each command-line argument passed to the script, shifting (removing) each one after handling it.
explanations.42: This runs 'docker system df' and uses awk to extract the fifth column (column $5) from the line containing 'Build Cache', which is the size of the cache.
explanations.46: The '@f' syntax splits the multi-line output from c_out into separate array elements, one line per element; the '(...)' syntax wraps it safely.
explanations.58: If the --all flag was passed, prune_all will be 1, triggering deep-clean mode; otherwise, the script uses standard mode for dangling images only.
explanations.70: This fetches the full image ID from Docker's inspect output, removes the 'sha256:' prefix, and truncates it to 12 characters to match Docker's short ID format.
explanations.74: The ':|' operator in Zsh performs array subtraction, removing all elements of used_imgs from all_imgs, leaving only the unused image IDs in i_ids.
explanations.105: This compares the step_name parameter with the current_step being displayed, so the script can highlight which step is about to execute next.
explanations.139: If the force flag is 1 (user passed -y), this function immediately returns success without prompting, auto-confirming the action.
explanations.140: The -q flag makes read silent (no echo), and the '?' after the string makes it a yes/no prompt that returns 0 for yes and 1 for no.
explanations.171: This uses eval to execute the img_cmd string (which was built earlier), allowing the command to expand properly with variables and special characters.
explanations.208: This checks if the buildx command exists by running its version subcommand; if it succeeds, the script uses the newer buildx-based pruning instead of the standard builder prune.
